definitions.definition: System software that manages computer hardware and software resources and provides common services for computer programs.
The always-running core of an operating system, which enforces protection between programs and users and manages memory and I/O devices.
Keeping several jobs in memory so that another job can use the CPU when one is blocked waiting for input or output.
Multitasking in which the operating system can interrupt a running thread, unlike the cooperative form where a thread runs until it yields control.
Operating system that schedules tasks for efficient use of the machine and may account for processor time and other resources.
Operating system that guarantees to process events or data by or at a specific moment in time.
Mode in which hardware checks that software executes only legal instructions, unlike the unrestricted powers of the kernel.
The programmatic way in which a computer program requests a service from the operating system.
Category of system calls for creating, ending, loading and running processes, waiting on events and allocating or freeing memory.
Category of system calls for creating, deleting, opening, closing, reading and writing files and managing their attributes.
Smallest sequence of programmed instructions that a scheduler can manage independently, usually as part of a process.
Thread that the kernel schedules directly; threads of one process share memory and files but each keeps its own stack and registers.
Thread managed and scheduled in userspace by a library, of which the kernel is unaware, so a blocking system call can stall all of them.
Model in which several threads exist within the context of one process, sharing its resources while executing independently.
Instance of a computer program that is being executed by one or many threads.
Data structure in which the operating system keeps most of the information about an active process.
Rapid swapping of the running process for another by the scheduler, which makes many processes appear to run at once on one processor.
Operating system module that selects the next jobs to be admitted into the system and which process runs next.
Admission scheduler that decides which jobs or processes are admitted to the ready queue, controlling the degree of multiprogramming.
Scheduler that temporarily removes processes from main memory and places them in secondary memory, freeing memory for others.
Scheduler that decides which of the ready, in-memory processes is to be executed next.
Policy in which the scheduler can forcibly remove a process from the CPU when it decides to allocate that CPU to another process.
The simplest scheduling algorithm, which runs processes in arrival order so long processes can delay short ones.
Scheduling that puts next in the queue the process with the least estimated processing time remaining, which requires time estimates.
Scheduling that assigns a fixed time unit per process and cycles through them, rescheduling unfinished processes after others get a turn.
Scheduling used when processes divide easily into groups, such as foreground interactive and background batch processes.
Module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler, performing the context switch.
Protected section of code that cannot be executed by more than one process or thread at a time.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Synchronization device used to control access to a common resource by multiple threads or processes.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Semaphore restricted to the values 0 and 1, often used to build locks.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Semaphore that allows an arbitrary resource count, tracking a pool of identical resources.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Semaphore operation that decrements the semaphore value by one and blocks the caller if the result is negative.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Semaphore operation that increments the semaphore value by one and wakes a waiting process if there is one.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Locking device that only the task that locked it is supposed to unlock.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Sharing of data between running processes in a computer system, or between multiple such systems.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Pipe that is treated like a file, which processes read and write as if it were an ordinary file.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Data stream similar to a socket that usually keeps message boundaries intact and lets processes communicate without being directly connected.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Method in which several processes are given access to the same block of memory, serving as a shared buffer for communication.
definitions.unitTitle: Process Synchronization and Inter Process Communication

definitions.definition: Situation in which no member of a group can proceed because each is waiting for another member.
Deadlock condition that resources are not shareable, so only one process at a time may use each resource.
Deadlock condition in which a process holds at least one resource while requesting others held elsewhere.
Deadlock condition in which each process waits for a resource held by another process in the cycle.
Approach that analyses each resource request to check whether granting it could still lead to deadlock, as the banker's algorithm does.
Approach that lets deadlocks occur and then examines the record of held and requested resources to find them.
Method of decoupling the memory organisation from the physical hardware, with virtual addresses translated to physical addresses.
Many small gaps between allocated memory blocks that can make the gaps unusable for new allocation requests.
Memory management scheme that adds a level of indirection between physical and logical addresses, letting a program's physical memory be non-contiguous.
Slot in physical memory that holds one page.
Structure that maps pages to page frames, letting scattered pages appear as one contiguous logical address space.
Event triggered when a process references a page that is not mapped to a frame in memory, passing control to the operating system.
Lazy scheme in which pages are loaded only when they are referenced.
Algorithm that decides which memory pages to page out to disk when a new page must be allocated.
Policy that swaps out the page whose next use will occur farthest in the future, which cannot be implemented in general.
Condition in a paging system whose memory is overcommitted, so it keeps moving pages to and from disk and handling page faults.
Service that governs file organisation and access, letting applications share mass storage.
Grouping that segregates files, also called a folder, which in a hierarchical system forms a tree structure.
Structure used by a file system to track which blocks of storage are free.
Disk scheduling method in which the arm travels in one direction servicing requests until none remain, then reverses.
Variant in which the head, after reaching the outer edge, returns to the start and services requests in the same direction again.
Variant that goes only as far as the final request in a direction, then reverses direction.
Variant that goes only as far as the final request, then jumps to the first request and continues in the same direction.
Feature that lets hardware subsystems access main memory independently of the CPU, so the CPU is not tied up during transfers.
Non-DMA approach in which the CPU moves the data itself, fully occupying it for the whole transfer.
Actively sampling the status of an external device, generally less efficient than waiting to be notified.
Abstract formal security model of protection state in which rows are subjects, columns are objects and cells list access rights.
List of permissions associated with a system resource, recording which subjects may perform which operations on it.
Communicable, unforgeable token of authority that pairs a reference to an object with a set of access rights.
Rule that each module must be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.
